speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
maintopic: RUSH-BAGOT AGREEMENT EXCHANGE OF NOTES AS TO APPLICATION AND INTERPRETATION IN LIGHT OF PRESENT CONDITIONS
speechtext:
At the request of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who is absent to-day, I wish to make the following statement:
1.	I am tabling, for the information of members of this house and for distribution, the following documents, both in English and in French:
Exchanges of notes, June 9, June 10, 1939, and October 30 and November 2, 1940, between the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs and the United States Minister to Canada, relating to the application and interpretation of the Rush-Bagot agreement.
2.	The Rush-Bagot agreement was embodied in an exchange of notes between His Majesty's minister at Washington and the United States Secretary of State, concerning the naval force to be maintained on the great lakes (Washington, 28-29, April 1817). This exchange is to be found in the publication filed in the Department of External Affairs, entitled "Treaties and Agreements Affecting Canada, in force between His Majesty and the United States of America, with subsidiary documents 1814-1925'' at pages 12 and 13. This volume is, of course, available

Rush-Bagot Agreement

to members of this house and to the public generally in all libraries, but for the convenience of the members of the house I shall read into the record a short excerpt from Sir Charles Bagot's note, which sets forth the operative provisions:
His Royal Highness, acting in the name and on the behalf of His Majesty, agrees, that the naval force to he maintained upon the American lakes by His Majesty and the government of the United States shall henceforth he confined to the following vessels on each side-that is:
On Lake Ontario to one vessel not exceeding one hundred tons burthen and armed with one eighteen-pound cannon.
On the upper lakes to two vessels not exceeding like burthen each and armed with like force.
On the waters of lake Champlain to one vessel not exceeding like burthen and armed with like force.
And His Royal Highness agrees, that all other armed vessels, on these lakes shall be forthwith dismantled, and that no other vessels of war shall be there built or armed.
His Royal Highness further agrees, that if either party should hereafter be desirous of annulling this stipulation, and should give notice to that effect to the other party, it shall cease to be binding after the expiration of six months from the date of such notice.
3.	In modern terminology it may be said that this was an agreement for quantitative and qualitative naval limitation on the great lakes. It is more than a century old and for a good while both Canada and the United States have mutually recognized that the technical scheme and definitions do not fit the actual present-day conditions, and that in fact they can reasonably and safely be waived without vitiating the underlying political spirit and objective which must be maintained.
4.	It is clear from a study of the documents relating to the negotiation of the agreement and its early history that the objective of the negotiators was to provide a solution of an immediate and urgent problem arising out of the war of 1812, and the terms of the agreement themselves support the view that its indefinite continuation in force was not anticipated. The governments of Canada and the United States have in fact from time to time by informal interchanges mutually recognized certain variations from the technical scheme and definitions. The agreement itself, however, has survived unchanged for more than one hundred and twenty yeans, and with the passage of time has assumed a symbolic importance in the eyes of the peoples of Canada and the United States.
5.	Recent negotiations between the Canadian and United States governments, affecting the agreement, took place in June, 1939. It was the desire of the United States government at that time to substitute other naval vessels of larger tonnage for certain naval vessels
'Mr. Crerar.]
already in the great lakes. The United States government also desired to use these vessels for training purposes and to equip them with armaments of heavier calibre than those permitted under the terms of the agreement. It was found possible to give effect to the wishes of the United States government by means of an informal exchange of notes and without the necessity of amending the agreement itself in any way.
6.	The outbreak of war brought about the need for a further understanding between the two countries with regard to the problem of naval construction on the great lakes. It was therefore suggested by the Canadian government that a further "interpretation" of the Rush-Bagot agreement be made, without involving any deviation from the basic intent of the agreement, namely that important naval vessels should not be built for service on the great lakes. An understanding was accordingly effected by an exchange of notes in November, 1940, to the effect that armaments might be installed on vessels built in great lakes shipyards, but dismantled for the voyage to the sea.
7.	It will be observed that the exchanges of notes, now being tabled, are in the nature of informal understandings as to the interpretation and application of the original agreement. They are not intended to rescind the Rush-Bagot agreement or to prejudice in any way the principles underlying that agreement or the underlying political spirit and objective which both countries have maintained. The position is continued whereby the great lakes are recognized as being an area in which naval armaments are not maintained by either country. At the same time, an arrangement has been worked out whereunder the resources of both countries within this area can be utilized to facilitate the defence, both of Canada and the United States, from external attack.
The documents which I now table contain the correspondence referred to in the statement I have just made, and they are submitted in both English and French.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PROVIDE FOR COOPERATION AS TO MEDICAL CARE OR COMPENSATION

speechtext:
Hon. H. A. BRUCE (Parkdale) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 21, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide that the unemployment insurance commission created by the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, shall cooperate with other authorities in the dominion or provinces for the purpose of collecting information concerning any plan for providing medical care or compensation in cases of ill-health.
The provisions were found in the Unemployment and Social Insurance Act, chapter 38 of
the statutes of 1935. This act, having been declared to be ultra vires by a majority of the supreme court, and subsequently by a judgment of the privy council delivered the 28th day of January, 1937, was repealed in 1940 by section 103 of chapter 44 of the statutes of that year, being the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940.
The competency of parliament to legislate in regard to unemployment insurance now has been settled by the amendment to the British North America Act of 1940. It is highly desirable to reintroduce these health provisions into our dominion law.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first
time.

subtopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL-IMPORTS OF MOTOR VEHICLES
FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL-IMPORTS OF MOTOR VEHICLES
speechtext:
1.	Has any change been made since the passing of the War Exchange Conservation Act in the conditions under which motor vehicles may be imported into Canada?
2.	If so, what is the nature of such change and for what purpose was it made?
3.	Has any ruling been made limiting an American motor vehicle manufacturer who might desire to establish a factory in Canada to a specified quota?
4.	If so, how was that quota determined?
5.	What was the purpose of such ruling?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL-IMPORTS OF MOTOR VEHICLES
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	Instead of refusal of all permits, permits are now granted for imports for three months based on a quota of 20 per cent of average imports for the comparable three monthly periods of the years 1938-1940.
3.	In addition to such limitations as may be imposed from time to time by the controllers of steel and machine tools, the motor vehicle controller, on the instructions of the government, has refused any new manufacturer the right to produce or assemble in
Questions

Canada more cars than can be imported under the import quota. Firms not producing cars in Canada prior to December 2, 1940 will not be permitted to produce more cars than they could obtain under import quota.
4.	This quota was made equal to the import quota the manufacturer would have received had the factory not been established in Canada.
5.	The prohibition of imports, in addition to imposing hardships, probably greater on the whole in the automobile business than in other businesses affected by the War Exchange Conservation Act, has also had the effect of leading some companies to consider setting up manufacturing facilities in Canada under conditions which cannot permit of economical production and at a time when machine tools and skilled labour are extremely scarce and required for war work.
When control of the entire industry was decided upon, the government took the view that the most effective plan was to allow the importation under permit of a very limited number of passenger automobiles as a part of a general plan of control. The plan will result not only in conserving machine tools and skilled labour for war work but also will save more foreign exchange than would have been possible, had new factories for the purpose of assembling cars in Canada with a low Canadian content been allowed to be established.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to a question connected with the sale of war savings certificates. I believe I might best put my question by reading from a letter appearing in the Toronto Globe and Mail of March 24. It says:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS AS TO METHOD OF DISTRIBUTION BT MAIL
speechtext: I have received many letters making representations similar to those made by the hon. member. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does the minister propose to give to-day the statement to which he alluded the other day with regard to the details of the training scheme, and particularly with regard to what methods are being employed to bring trainees who have completed their training into contact with those who are ready to employ them?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We are endeavouring to
see that the trainees receive employment at the earliest possible moment. Under the directorship of Mr. Thompson a committee has been set up which will keep in contact with the trainees as well as with prospective employers. I believe that everything possible is being done to see that trainees who have received their training shall be placed as soon as possible.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the official to whom the minister refers resident in Ottawa?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What machinery does he use to get in touch, say, with those who come out of the training classes in British Columbia?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: This work is carried on in cooperation with the provincial governments. Mr. Thompson was director of youth training and is now director of war emergency training. There is a seLup in each province which, subject to the supervision of Mr. Thompson, looks after the placing of these trainees. The hon. member realizes that in some provinces war industries are not concentrated to the extent they are in others and it is necessary that there should be a certain exchange of trainees, the trainees being brought to the industries. This whole matter was discussed at a conference which was held last week and at which I believe all . the provinces were represented. The whole plan was considered and I am told that the opinion was expressed that every possible step was being taken to see that trainees are brought into contact with industries that require them. In other words, it is a matter of dominion-provincial cooperation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is this committee a child of the provinces?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is perhaps a child of the provinces and the dominion. The provinces appointed representatives to attend this conference. Along with Mr. Thompson and Mr. Crawford, the latter in charge of the plant training plan in Ottawa, it was decided to secure the most effective cooperation in placing trainees as well as in developing trainees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What progress has been made in seeing that young men who have actually received this training get employment in the industries?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I shall have to supply my hon. friend with that information. I can give him the number being trained, if that would be of any assistance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think the minister
referred to that the other day.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have referred to that already. I would have to get the figures as to the actual number of trainees placed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Of course that is the test.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Quite. Generally speaking the placements have been most satisfactory. I shall place on Hansard the exact figures as to the number of placements. Sometimes it is a little difficult to get the proper records. For instance, a trainee may move from one point to another and neglect to advise us that he has been placed. We can give some figures, but we cannot undertake that they will be complete.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Before I left home at the beginning of February I attended the classes which were being held in my town and I was impressed with what I saw. These young men had acquired a considerable handiness and knowledge in a comparatively short time. But the principal and the instructors were worried over the next step, over how these lads in southern British Columbia were going to bring themselves into contact with industries which could use their services. I want to impress that fact upon the minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I appreciate that. I intended to give the hon. member for Yale some information in that regard. There were about fifty of these basic training schools to which he refers, and at that time definite plans were being made-I am speaking purely from memory-to place the trainees in an aircraft manufacturing plant in Vancouver. In other words, the plan is reasonably well coordinated. In one western city, for instance, we had 500 trainees. There was no employment for them there; and we had to move them, which we did, and I think every one of them has
War Appropriation Bill

been taken care of. With reference to the particular school to which my hon. friend refers, the plan is to find employment for these trainees in the aircraft manufacturing plant in Vancouver, with, I think, the Boeing company.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What number of men who have been discharged from the forces and what number of middle-aged men have received or are receiving training at the present time under these training schemes?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot give definite figures to the hon. member. I try to keep as up to date as I can on the number of trainees, but to answer that question I would have to have one of the officials of the department here.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Perhaps the minister could tell us what proportion of the trainees are young men, what proportion are men who have been discharged from the forces and what proportion are middle-aged.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would say-and I must put this in most general terms-that the training in the vocational schools is of young men from eighteen to thirty. There is, it is true, training of older-aged groups, but I could not advise my hon. friend as to the exact number.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Have active steps been taken to train these older men who could be fitted in perhaps much more easily than the younger men? Is that a factor at all?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes; it is a factor, but I would say that the great number of the trainees are between eighteen and thirty.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What provision has been
made for training ex-service men?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Under the war emergency training plan, preference is given to ex-service men who wish the training. It is definitely set forth in the war emergency training programme.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is any large number of them in training?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think it is a very great number, but there are some. The definite arrangement was made that preference would be given to them in the war emergency training programme.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
This is an important matter, and it has been published in the press as one of the achievements of the Department of National War Services. I am not very familiar with the programme myself, but as we are endeavouring to pass this bill to-day-at least that is the hope I entertain

I would ask the minister, before the committee stage is passed, to give us 
definite information on this training plan. I have the idea that in the maritime provinces this training programme has not been effective at all, but I should not like to speak too strongly as to that. I know an attempt was made in my own city to find work for these unemployed but no jobs could be found for them because no war industries are established and no new plants are being built in the maritimes. These men are willing to go to central Canada to find employment if they have to, but they have not had the opportunity.
I do not want to delay the passage of this bill, but we ought to know a little more about this training programme. It has been advertised to the country as one of the things we are going to do, and the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) is of importance. We have already brought back a large number of men. I have had some of them on my doorstep who cannot find employment.
The minister has also been advised of the situation existing in the county of Northumberland, New Brunswick, where unemployment threatens to be very, very serious this year due on account of a falling off in normal activities in that part of the country. Many of these unemployed are young men, and we have to do something about them. They cannot be left there to starve. Relief is cut off by the government of New Brunswick, and the municipality itself is so far in debt that it cannot possibly sustain these four or five thousand men who are threatened with unemployment if not actually now out of employment. I had hoped that this training scheme would be of great material benefit, and certainly, if labour is scarce in some places, work should be found for those who are trained. We have undertaken to train these young men, and the application of the scheme should be national, embracing the whole country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I know the situation in the county of Northumberland to which the hon. leader of the opposition refers. It is a matter about which he and I have conversed, but I doubt if the situation there is one that could properly come under the training plan. I think it would have to come under some such thing as he suggested, namely, the building of wooden ships or some definite activity of that kind.
With regard to New Brunswick generally, it is true that there are not as many receiving training in that province as there are in some other provinces. Perhaps I might give the figures for New Brunswick. The number in training on February 1 was 212; the number enrolled in February was 91. I agree that in

War Appropriation Bill
comparison with the total figures that is not a large number. The number who left during the month was thirty-seven. The number training at the end of February was 266.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How many of them were placed?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There were twenty-four finished but not placed. That would mean that the number placed was forty-six. That is not a large number, I must admit, as compared with other provinces. It might be fair to the committee for me to put on Hansard a general statement as to the training plan as the leader of the opposition has suggested, and with the permission of the committee I shall follow my notes pretty closely.
The emergency war training programme has its legal basis in the Youth Training Act. This act, passed in 1939, provided grants to the provinces to meet 50 per cent of the cost of training and rehabilitating unemployed youth. With the outbreak of war, emphasis in training necessarily shifted from rehabilitation to the fitting of young persons to meet the demand for semi-skilled and skilled labour in war production. Although the programme was changed in this way it has continued to operate under the youth training legislation. The youth training work proper has rapidly declined, while the special training for war occupations has been so expanded that additional war appropriations have been secured to finance the expansion of the work. The provinces have made their technical schools and equipment available to the dominion for the work of the programme, while about 85 per cent of the additional expense involved is being met by the dominion government.
The war emergency training has two phases:
(1) Training in vocational schools.
(2) Training in industry.
The former is in charge of Mr. R. F. Thompson, dominion director of youth training; the latter phase has been assigned to Mr. A. W. Crawford, former dominion director of technical education, who has been loaned to the dominion government by the Ontario department of labour.
With regard to the vocational schools, we were fortunate in having laid a foundation for further expansion in the experience already had in youth training. New curricula for war production occupations were drawn up, suitable instructors were secured, and many of the schools were placed on a two-shift and even on a three-shift basis. To date the supply of applicants for training has been adequate and the programme has proceeded according to schedule. It is proposed to train
50,000	persons for industry and the armed forces in the 75 vocational schools in the
present calendar year-14,000 for the army,
6,000	for the air force and 30,000 for industry- and I am glad to report that in the first two months of the year this schedule is being met.
The numbers in training were:
At the first of January, 6,585.
At the first of February, 10,381.
At the first of March, 11,422.
Since the average duration of the courses is about three months, this means that an average of about 4,000 persons can be graduated monthly. Moreover, the output of trainees can be expanded as the need arises. In the summer vacation months, when the ordinary day pupils of the schools are on vacation, another shift of war production trainees can be introduced. We are also informed by the provincial authorities that, on short notice, the facilities will permit the training of perhaps 25 per cent more persons. Moreover, new centres may be added if required. I am confident that our objective of 50,000 vocational school graduates for service in war production will be attained.
That figure was arrived at, as probably some members of this committee know, as a result of the investigation of the interdepartmental committee on labour supply, comprising various departments of the government interested in it.
With respect to the plant training phase of the programme it is difficult to speak in the same precise terms. No governmental assistance is being given to employers to meet the cost of training new workers. Up to the moment we have adopted the position that the cost of training in industry should be borne by industry itself. This being so, we have no control of the activities in this direction and are unable to insist upon detailed statistical reports covering the extent and nature of their training plans.
While available figures indicate that the estimate of 50,000 trainees in industrial plants will be exceeded, it should be borne in mind that the constantly changing situation in each industrial establishment makes it impossible to predict the future with any great degree of certainty.
There is some difficulty in getting the figures from the industrial plants. For instance, in the case of one large firm where, I know, they are training about 500 men, they say, "We are not training them, because they are not in a plant school; they are being trained in the plant itself." In the case of other industries, every man they take on will be in training under direction, no matter how short the training that is given. The result is that it is a little difficult to get figures for the industrial plant schools.
War Appropriation Bill

The point is this, however. I feel that the programme is doing well. The reports I obtain on it are that we shall have no difficulty and will train in the vocational schools over 50,000 during the calendar year ind will train in the plant schools also 50,000 luring the calendar year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is a very substantial programme, and I wish it every success. What, in the opinion of the officials of the minister's department, is the proper course to pursue; is it better to have these trainees trained in the technical schools, or in the plant schools, or in the industry itself? The good old-fashioned system of apprenticeship obtained in this country for many years and I always regretted that it went on to the scrap hill. I would assume that all three methods might properly be utilized and that the training in technical schools is, possibly, the least conducive to immediate employment. That is just a hazard, a guess. The objective, of course, is to put these men to work in the appropriate place, so that they may become self-sustaining and preserve their self-respect and become good citizens. The crux or true test of any of these schemes is the success which has been achieved in finding employment, and the minister cannot give us very much information on that at the moment. I should like to know what the results are.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Of course all three plans
which the leader of the opposition suggests, namely the technical school, the plant school, and the apprenticeship system, have been worked. The difficulty with apprenticeship is the time it takes, a matter of four or five years; and necessarily the number of apprentices is limited. The vocational schools are giving training in respect of branches of industry in which it appears that there will be the first shortage of labour; in the matter of welding of various kinds we are dealing with those in an endeavour to avoid a shortage. In the plant schools-and perhaps it is a misnomer to call them "schools"-or in the plants, the training they are giving is directly related to the work which they are going to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The particular industry.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Quite true, the particular industry. We are trying through the vocational schools to anticipate the demand which there will be for the scarcer varieties of labour. For instance, we are turning out a great number of aircraft mechanics for the air force and a great number for the aircraft manufacturing companies. We are endeavouring to fill the gap which is caused by the lack

of certain forms of skilled labour, such as welders, not related to one particular industry but to a number of industries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would the minister give the figures for Nova Scotia? My experience with the training plan in that province is that it is as hard to get into those schools as it is to get into the university.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Well,
that ought not to be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: For instance, over the weekend I had personal letters from 115 boys in one ward in the town of Glace Bay. They were advised to write the government, and they wrote me. Their ages range from nineteen to thirty years. They have never had a job, and they are endeavouring to get some information as to how they can take advantage of these schools, or whether there is the possibility of employing them somewhere. From another ward in the same town there were forty-seven individual letters registering complaints. Under whose supervision in Nova Scotia, is the work being carried on, and what are the figures relating to trainees?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I shall be glad to give the hon. member the figures for Nova Scotia. I cannot recall offhand the name of the particular individual in that province who is in charge. The number in training at the first of the month was 158; the number enrolled during the month is 97; the number in training at the end of the month is 253. The industrial schools in Nova Scotia are, the Halifax, N.S., technical college, and the New Glasgow training centre, trainees' training centre; and for the army, the Halifax, N.S., technical college, and, at New Glasgow, the training centre.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If a young man wants
to get into the big central school in Toronto, by what procedure does he obtain that privilege?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would say, Mr. Chairman, that the procedure would be to apply to the school; and if there should be any difficulty in getting in, he would be at perfect liberty to take it up with the Ontario authorities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My information is that
there is great difficulty in getting into these schools, that young men who apply are told that they might get in six months hence or nine months hence, but that at present the classes are filled up. By what method are selections made of those who enrol?
I have had a great deal of experience with such work as is taught in the technical school, particularly that relating to iron and steel,

War Appropriation Bill
and I do not know just how much a young man could learn in the length of time which a course in that particular work, according to what I read in the papers, is supposed to cover. After all, it takes time to train expert machinists, tool makers, die makers, and the like. In my day a man had to work two or three years, or longer, before he learned enough to be really worth much. Are we going to get out of this technical training scheme everything we should get out of it so far as the prosecution of the war is concerned? -for that is the real purpose of it. A young man who gets a smattering in two or three months in a technical school might be helpful if he went to work in a plant. I have no doubt the teachers in those schools are doing everything they can, working early and late and on Saturdays to try to fill the gap. I remember a few years ago telling the then minister of labour that it was high time some effort was made to retain in this country expert mechanics who at that time were going to England to work in munitions plants-as tool and die makers, experts of particularly high type-but nothing was done. I feel that what the minister is trying to do should be appreciated, and I hope something is coming out of it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The particular school to which my hon. friend refers-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The Central Technical
School.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would not be surprised if difficulty were being experienced in getting in there; it is pretty well filled up. Por instance, there were 391 trainees at the first of the month, and 272 joined during the month. It is one of the major schools. They probably have a waiting list.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, I tried to get one
m myself.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In regard to the training, we are giving three months' training on an average. As the hon. member says, you could not turn out a highly skilled tool and die maker in that time, such as you used to get under the apprenticeship system. What we are trying to do is to give the fundamental knowledge, to try to grade up, so to speak, and at least teach them the fundamentals to make them useful in the plant. As to how useful they are, the only information I have comes from those into whose employ they go, and I would say that employers have been uniformly favourable in their comments on the helpfulness of the training and the advantages to industry which are flowing from this work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is there any shortage of instructors?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We could perhaps train more men if we had more instructors and more equipment. If there are any shortages it is in instructors and equipment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister's answer to my question would indicate that in Nova Scotia the whole scheme is concentrated in one end of the province. The figures are very low. So far as the training of industrial workers is concerned or of boys who are to take part in future industry -he might well move that Halifax school down to the other end of the country where there is the greatest concentration of industry as well as the greatest number of unemployed boys. It would save money for the government, transporting men from one end of the province to the other. In addition you have the big steel plant down there, and if the minister is receiving the cooperation from industry that he should be receiving that is the proper place to train the trainees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What would happen in the other end of the province?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You have practically everything there now; that is the trouble. The last time I was home I met hundreds of these boys in our end of the country who had absolutely no knowledge of the scheme or who was handling it or whom to get in touch with to inquire about it. There is very little advertising in Nova Scotia with respect to it. I suggest that an examination of that question in Nova Scotia is necessary. As I see it, the training of industrial workers is being done at the wrong end of the country. The whole thing is concentrated in Halifax. The few times I have been in Halifax since the outbreak of the war I found everything so congested that one did not know what he was doing or where he was going.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have had the opportunity of visiting the Halifax technical school on at least two occasions. I have been immensely impressed with the training they are giving and the work they are doing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is a good school, but in the wrong place.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am not objecting to that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: Perhaps I might say just one word with reference to my hon. friend's remark that the four months training is interfering with industry. speechtext:
The rule is that the
veterans are given the preference in connection with training. Those over forty years of age and the women are next. There are three classes we do not ask for, and the fourth is the group from forty years down to eighteen. There is only one class in that group whom we are calling to take training and that is those twenty-one years of age, and of those the army says "We do not want and will agree to the postponement of those who are twenty-one years of age and who are engaged in key posts in essential war industry." My hon. friend I think is making it harder than it really is, because the army, as I have said time and again and now repeat, is not in competition with industiy but in cooperation with it, and when we narrow our requirements for compulsory training down to the twenty-one year old class and say that of that class we will postpone calling, if necessary, those who are key men, and still leave all these other classes from eighteen to forty, I do not think my hon. friend has much ground for assuming that there is conflict.
Furthermore, this whole matter has been the subject of discussion by the labour coordination committee which is composed, not only of representatives of labour and representatives of the army, but of representatives of labour, representatives of the defence services, representatives of the national war services and representatives of the Department of Munitions and Supply. They all come together on that committee, and that committee is recommending this course. My hon. friend has a right to press as hard as he can to see that that is working, but on the principles which have been laid down he will find there is not very much competition between labour and the army training plan, and I want him to take what I say at one hundred per cent. I am a little concerned as to whether there is a welfare service which will take him under its wing and show him just what is available. There is hardly a member of this committee who has not found from time to time that he did not know until some time afterwards what vacancies were open in certain lines. We have a definite responsibility and duty in this regard to the men discharged in this war. It is all very well to say that we will try to find them jobs. But the difficulty is that many of them are not trained for any particular employment. Perhaps before the war they were unemployed for a number of years, and their training had not been brought up to date, because the trained man of fifteen years ago in certain

In view of the fact that this is a matter which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance, I would ask him certain questions regarding advances to private corporations. I find that out of the many millions of dollars advanced to private corporations, the only advance to Saskatchewan is to the M. and C. Aviation company of Prince Albert, which received some $81,000 for overhauling a base for the air force, and $450 for office furniture. Have there been any applications from Saskatchewan for advances to private corporations to permit them to build additions to plants so as to make provision for the filling of war orders?
Who determines the amount to be advanced to the different companies by way of capital assistance?
How are the allotments made?
Why is it that in certain instances among companies in the same industry exceptionally large advances are made to some, while others receive only comparatively small advances, each of the companies being capitalized on about the same basis?
Would the minister explain whether or not this system of advancing moneys to private corporations is in effect in the United Kingdom?
Upon whose recommendation was this system brought into effect?
In view of the fact that many millions of dollars have been advanced to these private corporations, as an incentive or by way of assistance, has consideration been given by the government to the powers it possesses under the National Resources Mobilization Act to take over those plants, or to have them operated by private corporations throughout the period of the war, under the direction and supervision of the government?
By these questions I direct the attention of the minister to the type of information to which I believe the committee is entitled.
On whose recommendations are these advances made?
Who are the trustees who look after the advancing of moneys, and the collection thereof?

In other words, I want a general statement of the whole situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I can give a fairly general statement. First, I would point out that this is a matter administered by the Department of Munitions and Supply, not by the Department of Finance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But the Department of Finance has to find the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes. The Department of Munitions and Supply applies to the treasury board for the approval of draft estimates which, in effect, is approval of certain of the advances, as those advances are required, and that department supplies the Department of Finance with information which makes a case for the approval of the draft estimates, whereupon the estimates are approved, and taken out of the war appropriation. This is done by the treasury board.
After that, when the agreement is made with the particular company to which the advance is made, authorization for that agreement is obtained by order in council. Thousands of these orders in council go through. Of course there are not thousands which relate to capital advances, but there are thousands relating to agreements made by the Department of Munitions and Supply with companies and firms throughout Canada. They go to council, as a matter of fact, there is a committee of council, known as the government business committee, which examines these recommendations to council. If there is anything extraordinary or unusual about them, they are brought to the attention of council as a whole. If we did not adopt some such procedure, council would be so greatly overtaxed that it would never finish the work it has to do.
So far as the Department of Finance and council are concerned, there are those two stages. First, there is approval of the draft estimate. This does not approve the agreement with the company, but merely makes the money available, and places the matter in the same position as if it were an amount voted by parliament. After this, the Department of Munitions and Supply must make a recommendation to council for approval of the particular agreement it is making with the private company. There are those two stages. The real work, however, is done in the Department of Munitions and Supply. The theory underlying the practice is that they have to get ahead; they have to get action. They have to have things manufactured in Canada, and must get things done.

Yes, for the purpose of
getting munitions and supplies-it may be a supply of chemicals, or a wide variety of other goods. They do it for the purpose of getting these facilities for the British government or for the Canadian government. If facilities for making the particular type of munitions do not exist and they have to be supplied, the question then arises as to what is the best, the most effective way of getting those facilities established.
There is no use in going to a private corporation and telling them to take a chance, to risk their capital, to put up one or two million dollars because they owe it to their country to risk it. They probably will reply that -they cannot afford to put up two million dollars, run their plant for a year and a half or two years, and then find it is not worth anything or is not any good. We have to have some better arrangement than that. Therefore all kinds of arrangements have been made. Sometimes they are willing to put up their own money provided they are allowed to write it off within a certain period, to charge it off to operating revenue. In that event there is no advance from the government; the only thing they get from the government is a market. Either the British or the Canadian government buy their products, and it is with that money that they pay for the plant in the year or two years or three years, as the case may be. In some instances this is not good enough for them and it is necessary for the government to lend them money. Sometimes the government will build the plant and retain ownership in it, or sometimes it will put up an extension to the plant. As a matter of fact, there is no consistent principle followed. It is not a government ownership system and it is not a private ownership system; it is whatever system will get results.
The Department of Munitions and Supply have a number of exceptionally able men who have had a tremendous amount of business experience. They have a large legal staff and a number of trained accountants. I have been impressed with the great ingenuity and ability which they have displayed in making these arrangements, and in getting the wheels of industry turning. Canada is not primarily an industrial country, but the strides which have been made are tremendous.
I was asked if there had been applications from Saskatchewan. I do not know whether there have been applications; I shall have to find that out. It is quite possible that there have been applications and that these have been turned down.

As I
recollect it-and I speak subject to correction -during the last war the government did not advance into the new fields which have been taken over by the present government. In order to encourage industrialists to produce munitions, which was the big item-we have gone into many other things since-if the government was satisfied as to their capabilities, plant and so on, a trial order would be given at a high price. If they were successful with that order, then the order was renewed at a progressively lower rate, until it was got down to a decent basis. I have often wondered whether there might not be opportunity for abuse in connection with this writing off for depreciation. I understand that most of these depreciation accounts are to be taken up in two years.
I should like to refer to another governmental activity in connection with the providing of additional storage facilities for wheat. In that connection the government has made what I consider is a most generous gesture to the elevator companies by allowing them to write off the cost of structures in two years. I was reading the order in council to-day. .These companies are being allowed to write off in two years the cost of new structures which may be good for from five to ten years.

speechtext: There are some limitations. At the moment I am not critical of that. I think some inducements had to be offered in order to have them make the necessary capital expenditures. I discussed this matter informally with the Minister of Mines and Resources, and I told him that I thought the principle was one which the government would have to recognize, but 1 certainly did not visualize a write-off in two years. That, however, is only by the way. What care is the government taking to protect the income tax branch with respect to these write-offs for depreciation by industrial plants? For instance, do they take into account what salvage value there might be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The McTague board is the one that sanctions the write-off arrangements. The first thing this board does is to estimate the salvage value at the end of the period for which the write-off is allowed. For instance, if the period is three years and it is estimated that the salvage value will be 25 per cent, then at the end of the three years they permit a write-off of only 75 per cent, which would be 25 per cent per annum for the three years. Then, after that, I assume there would be the regular write-off at income tax rates.
The public is, however, protected in connection with these arrangements in two ways. In the first place, if munitions are being supplied to the government-and the government will be the purchaser-as soon as the supplier has had his plant completely depreciated, his costs drop. That write-off disappears as an element of cost, and the price that he can get from the government comes down. That is protection No. 1. Protection No. 2 is that if there should be an intervening period where that was not the situation, the excess profits tax comes in and takes 79J per cent of his excess profits for the dominion, and he also has to pay from 5 to 10 per cent of those profits to the province, the rate depending upon where he is. So industry is pretty well under control, even with these write-offs.

May I ask the Minister of Labour if an item in the Ottawa Morning Journal of Saturday last has been called to his attention? It is headed "Enough Ontario Labour" and reads:
Labour Minister Norman Hipel said to-day that no importation of labour from outside Ontario is needed for the province's war industry except in such highly-skilled trades as tool and die-making.
That can be interpreted as a notice from the government of Ontario to the people of

War Appropriation Bill

the rest of Canada that the people of Ontario want a monopoly of employment in Canada's war industry, for war industry is largely situated in that province.
Last June I made some inquiries and learned that employment in Ontario was arranged for the proprietors of those war industries through the Ontario government employment offices, and I was likewise informed that in order to get employment through the Ontario government employment offices one had to be a resident of that province for two years.
I protested to the Minister of Labour at that time, and I believe that this regulation was relaxed, but we have here again a warning from Ontario's minister of labour to the rest of the people of Canada to stay out of Ontario because "you are not wanted, you are not required, you are not needed, for we demand for Ontario residents a monopoly of employment in Ontario's war industry".
How does that affect us in other parts of Canada? In my own city of Regina, with a population of 55,000 people, we have, on relief, 1,044 men who are fit for war work. They are not unemployable. They are healthy vigorous men, heads of families, who desire and require work in order to maintain themselves and their families. As an alternative to employment they must be provided with relief. The same condition prevails in Moose Jaw and in practically every other urban centre in Saskatchewan. Frankly, we do not like notices such as the one I have just read from the minister of labour of Ontario that that province intends to monopolize labour employment in Canada's war industry.
Further, the greater part of the moneys that have been advanced to subsidize war industry has been invested in Ontario, and the greater part of the army training, of the air training programme, is centred in Ontario. Likewise, the great military camps are centred in Ontario. An analysis of pay and allowances shows that the great bulk of that sum also goes to Ontario.
What is the situation in our province? War conditions or the particular facts concerning war strategy make it impossible or inadvisable for us to sell our wheat; freight rates, or the lack of power or the lack of this or that also make it impossible for war industries to be established in Saskatchewan, so we are told. The necessities of dominion government finance also make it necessary to refuse any further advances for relief.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to visualize the situation of Saskatchewan where there are one million people anxious and willing
and equipped to do their part in this war effort and to pull their full weight. They are precluded from so doing by the facts just enumerated and emphasized now by an announcement such as I have just read. If that situation continues, there is going to be a definite protest, couched in more definite language, from all the rest of Canada and a demand that this centralization of war industry shall cease, that war industry be decentralized and spread out so that all the people of Canada will be given a chance to do theii part.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to make any speech, but my idea will be to mention just a few facts especially relating to the bill which is now before the committee. It is entitled "An act for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security." The word "security" must have

War Appropriation Bill
a meaning, and the meaning should be that there should be protection for every part of the country. I wonder what protection the part of the country in which I live and which I represent in this house may have at the present time against any possible attack by land or air or water. In other words, I should like to know what is the military protection for the city of Riviere du Loup and the county of Temiscouata. I have made representation to the Department of National Defence for a military training centre, a military camp in the vicinity of Riviere du Loup, and the experts of the department have not yet answered. I had occasion some years ago, when the estimates of the Department of National Defence were increased for the first time, to say what I thought of those experts, and I shall judge them after they have given an answer and I see what it is.
In connection with all that expenditure there is something that should not be overlooked. I shall quote a few words spoken by a great lady who has a very clear mind and a very generous heart. My quotation is from the Montreal Gazette of October 8 last year. The heading is:
Home Services must be continued declares H.R.H. Princess Alice.
Holds they are no less important than war projects though they lack glamour-Urges aid to Magdalen islands-Speaks to Women's Canadian club.
The report continues:
No less important than direct war work, though it lacked glamour and romance, was the task of keeping important home services going, said Her Royal Highness Princess Alice when yesterday she addressed the luncheon meeting of the Women's Canadian club held in the Windsor hotel. She stated that it was "more than futile" to spend all the money available on the actual war effort to the neglect of essential home services, for when peace came the youth of the country then would be wholly unfitted to share in the great task which lay before it.
In saying that, Her Royal Highness expressed what many people in every part of this country are thinking.
An objection that is made by some people is that we have not enough trained men. Of course they consider only those who live in big cities, they pay no attention to the skilled workmen who live in smaller communities or rural districts. Anyone who lives in the country knows that there are trained men of great ability in such places, but they have no opportunity to work on war projects because they are not residents of a city w'here there is some large war expenditure.
I shall now make a few suggestions to the government regarding what could be done to give to men of good-will an opportunity to do their share even if, for physical or other
reasons, they are unable to enlist. This afternoon I received a pamphlet about advertising good roads, a short cut to Alaska. Of course Alaska belongs to the United States and there is a route projected from there to Alaska. But there are other routes of no less importance; from the United States to the St. Lawrence there are three. There is the King Edward VII highway between Montreal and Rouse's Point; there is the Levis-Jackson route, and, finally, there is a route from Madawaska, Maine, to Riviere du Loup through Edmundston. This is an old military road, and it should be maintained in good order now that we are supposed to receive military supplies from the United States by truck. It may surprise the committee to know that the province of Ontario has received more than 814,000,000 for the trans-Canada highway, and has a very big project for this year, while the province of Quebec until last year received only 8400,000 for the same project. We did not have our share, and since we hear now only about war projects, I do not see why the government does not take this opportunity to redress the wrong that has been done to the province of Quebec in the past, by spending a certain amount of money on repairing and putting in good order the military route between Edmundston and Riviere du Loup and keeping it open in winter time.
