I am glad to hear my
hon. friend say that because he knows the place very well; he travels there often and he knows it is an old military road. There is no reason why it should not be made up to date immediately. It would be at the same time an evidence of good-will to our neighbours who are our allies and associates in this war.
Then, with regard to the manufacture of wooden boxes for shells, immediately after the start of the war there was no question of manufacturing wooden boxes for shells; the shells were wrapped in corrugated paper, just like bottles of Scotch. I wonder whether that was done by Mr. Dunning or on his advice, because he was interested in the Consolidated Paper company and other pulp companies, or Mr. Belnap or Mr. Crabtree or another. It would help the smaller industries in various parts of the country if those boxes were made in the same way as in the last war. I understand that now the Department of Munitions and Supply is starting to do it again.
Another thing that some of my friends know and that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition knows also is that ships have
War Appropriation Bill

already been built in the estuary of the Riviere du Loup by the Fraser company. I remember that a steamship was built there. It is a fine place to build ships, and I do not see why our people should not be given the same opportunity that is given other people to build ships in other parts of the country. There are before the government at the present time requests that this work be carried on there, as well as requests for dry docks at that point, and I believe these projects would further our war effort and at the same time give many more people an opportunity to do their share.
I might leave the matter at that. I am very sorry the Minister of National Defence is not in his place, but perhaps at another time I may ask further questions. In any event I have placed these facts on record. I would say further that we must have regard to the unemployable unemployed in our country, as well as to those who are unemployed at the present time although able and willing to work. They must be given a chance. Canada does not consist only of the capital cities of the provinces and the great centres of population; Canada is more than that. Canada is every part of this country from ocean to ocean. War industry must be decentralized to as great an extent as possible. These industries should be located not only in the constituencies represented in this house by ministers but also in the constituencies represented by private members. I say that because in all constituencies the people are subscribing to drives of all kinds, and the men are enlisting. In Riviere du Loup, for instance, with a population of 9,000, some 550 men have enlisted voluntarily in the army, the air force and the navy, which is an average of over six per cent. We must not overlook the fact that Canada is a large country; that it is represented here by 245 members, and that each constituency is entitled to have a share in the work necessary to win the war.
The men now unemployed must not be allowed to starve after April 1, although it has been decided that this government will not contribute in any way to relief after that date. I would direct the attention of members of the government to certain facts which I placed on Hansard last year, and I urge as strongly as possible that we follow as closely as we can what is being done for the unemployed in the United States. Many boys have been found unfit for army service because they have not been properly fed. That was because the unemployed did not have enough to eat and did not receive the medical attention to which they were entitled, and 
which the unemployed were given in the United States. This is a humanitarian business, and the country receives some benefit in return. I was appalled at the proportion of young boys who were found medically unfit for military service. Two of the war ministers stated that about one-third of those who applied for enlistment were not accepted for physical reasons. In a country like ours, where the climate is so healthful, there is no excuse for that sort of thing. Often I have heard hon. gentlemen from the west say that in this country where the elevators are full of grain there is no reason for anyone to die of hunger, and I agree with that. In my humble view the government should act as a pendulum and try to correct all wrongs of this kind. This is not entirely a question of charity, because the country will receive much in return. For one thing, if the unemployed are treated as they should be, the proportion of men fit for military service will be greatly increased.
There is another aspect of the matter. If no consideration is given our young people in all parts of the country, there will be unrest which will grow deeper and deeper until eventually it may cause great social problems. That is my fear. Our own citizens should be given the first opportunity to earn money in this country. At the present time Canada is a dumping ground for all the countries of the world, and sometimes the fact that a man is a Canadian is an obstacle to his appointment to the civil service, or to consideration which is given other people. I do not mean that we should be other than generous to those who suffer now, but when it comes to filling a position and there is available a Canadian citizen who is competent to do the work, I do not see why he should not get the job.
According to some of the sessional papers, in 1931 there were 3,500 people employed in the Post Office Department who were not born in Canada. In 1937 that number had increased to over 7,000, and now I wonder whether if it is not 10,000. I do not place the blame for this on anyone in particular, but I find it strange that 10,000 people not born in Canada should find jobs in one department of this government while many of our own people are still unemployed. The conclusion is, I think, obvious. It is that we must think first as Canadians. When we give help to Great Britain or any other friendly country in the world we must do all we can; we must do our utmost for the very worthy cause for which we are fighting, but on the other hand

War Appropriation Bill
we must never forget that we are Canadians and that we must give our own people the first chance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there was lengthy discussion when the resolution preceding this bill was in the committee stage, yet this evening I feel that before this bill passes it is necessary that I should say something about one section in particular. Section 2 of the bill mentions the security, order and welfare of Canada. I have sat through these last few days listening to a debate, much of which has had to deal with technical matters. I feel there are some points concerning the welfare of Canada itself which perhaps have not received from the committee the amount of consideration that they should have. It was most encouraging this evening to hear the hon. member for Temiscouata quote the words of the Princess Alice, who said that although these matters of concern to the people of Canada are not perhaps as glamorous as some others, yet they are necessary. It is of those things I wish to speak.
The very first time I spoke in the house I said I would try always to speak in the interests of the lives of the Canadian people. To be consistent, I must continue in that direction. In January, 1941, President Roosevelt said that this was no time to stop thinking about the social and economic problems which are the root cause of the social revolution which is to-day a factor of supreme importance in the world. We can never forget, even in a time of crisis such as this, the needs of our own people.
I was greatly alarmed the other day when I listened to the remarks of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) when he told the house about the number of young men unfit for service. On Monday, March 17 the minister said, as reported at page 1605:
There will be for training this year 93,000 young men of the age of 21 years. Without hesitation one can knock off 33 per cent of those as being unfit even for military training camps. That is, they would be placed in classes C-l or C, and unfit to walk five miles.
If so large a proportion of the men called for military service must be classified as C or C-l, then what must be the proportion of our civilian population who are to-day unfit because of ill health to help carry the burden of the war effort. We are fighting a war which not only falls upon the shoulders of the young men in uniform, but is placed upon the shoulders of the civilian population. For this reason the question of the health of our people in these years is one of primary importance.
During the last war there were people who enjoyed what might be called comparative 14873-115
prosperity; yet after that war, when we went down into the slough of depression they suffered unduly. This war is being fought after a period of depression, during which time the health of the people of Canada suffered. I feel that, as time goes on, the health of our people will suffer even more- not only in the immediate future, but after this war is over. We must not forget these things.
After the last war we had the money to pay interest on the debt which accumulated during the war. But during the years of depression we did not have' sufficient money to start a national health scheme. I am wondering whether perhaps right here and now is not the proper time and place to begin thinking about the problem of national health. We ought not to leave it until after this war is over.
Recently I came across a pamphlet entitled "The Fight For Life," written by Grant Lathe, M.D., who places on record some startling figures. Among other things he said that in Canada to-day we are needlessly losing many of our children. He said that a needless infant death occurs every hour. There would be
6.500	more Canadian babies alive to-day if the rest of the country had enjoyed as low a rate of infant mortality as does British Columbia. He says that 59'9 persons out of every 100,000 of the population die each year from tuberculosis. That makes an average of
7.500	persons a year. He states that in Canada there is a shortage of 3,500 beds for patients suffering from tuberculosis. He states, too, that syphilis in Canada is causing more than 3,000 deaths each year, and that in 1937 the total number of new cases stood at more than 8,000. Canada has almost as many new cases of syphilis as has Great Britain, despite the fact that Great Britain has a population four times as great as ours. He points out that mental hospital accommodation in Canada falls short of requirements in the amount of 8,657 beds. Dementia praecox takes a terrible toll of our young people. Every fourth hospital bed in Canada is occupied by a person suffering from this disease. He goes on to point out that more young people enter our mental asylums than enter our universities. The inadequacy of existing public health service in Canada is shown by the fact that the average expenditure by municipal departments of health for public health services was only fifty-one cents per person per annum. Yet the minimum necessary is placed at one dollar per person per annum. Only one city in Canada goes beyond that amount. That is the city of Toronto, which shows a rate of $1.21 per person. On the

War Appropriation Bill

other hand, Halifax spends only about twenty-two cents. Roughly, two-thirds of our Canadian citizens, or about 66 per cent, are unable to afford the medical care which should be theirs, as human beings.
When we consider these things we feel there is no time like the present for the government really taking into consideration the needs of the people and devoting some of this huge appropriation to the beginning of a health scheme in Canada which would give our people an opportunity to maintain that vigour which is so necessary, if they are to give their very best in the war effort, as they are being asked to do.
There is one other factor which I feel is of the utmost importance. We are fighting a war to preserve and to extend democracy. There is no place where the principles of democracy can be better taught than among our children in the schools of the nation. That must be done, if we are to preserve democracy, because democracy is founded upon the premise that we shall have an intelligent and educated people, and by discussion we shall decide what shall be done. That cannot be effected if we have a population part of which is to be denied the right of education.
Recently the Canadian Teachers' Federation published a bulletin which I believe would be of interest to hon. members. I feel that I could not do better than turn to that group for ideas concerning what should be done in connection with education. As a body they have information on the subject. The federation say they are concerned with the fact that Canada to-day is setting a course which in the future may lead through uncharted seas, and that we are not giving the solicitude to education which as a nation we should give. Education more than any other agency can, by its power, save the ship of democracy, or, by its impotence, scuttle the ship.
The brief which should have been submitted to the dominion-provincial relations conference contains a number of statements about the condition of education in Canada. I believe there was in the Sirois report a statement to the effect that in some parts of Canada education has been terribly neglected and that children in the various provinces do not have equal opportunities. I find this in the brief:
The present system of financial support for education in Canada is such that only two provinces (Ontario and British Columbia) can take rank in the upper half of the American states in per-pupil expenditure, while four provinces (Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick) must rank in the lowest quartile of the American states.
It goes on to say that about 49 per cent of all Canadian teachers receive less than $770

per annum, which is below the average initial salary of women teachers in most British countries. In 1938, over 32 per cent of Canadian teachers were paid less than $600 per annum. The teachers' federation say that in England in 1914, after the start of the war, the British parliament voted an increase of about six millions for education. They go on to say that in Canada they feel that the dominion government should-I believe that a body of this kind has every right to state these things-make available a substantial sum, and they suggest $10,000,000 annually, as a grant in aid for education to those provinces which are found by a competent survey to be deficient in tax-paying ability.
I know that to many people these things do not rank with the same importance as the industrial production for our war effort. Yet I cannot help but stress the fact that in a war to preserve democracy these things are of fundamental importance and we cannot afford to neglect them at any time. During this debate we have had many examples of politics, but I feel that to-day it is not politics that matter so much as statesmanship. We should not be thinking of the present or of the next few months; we should be thinking of statesmanship of the future; we should be thinking of the generations which are to come and which will benefit from the things for which we are fighting to-day.
After all, the children of this countiy cannot speak for themselves. Many children throughout the dominion have no way of knowing that they have unequal chances; they have no way of knowing that they are being deprived of opportunities which would benefit them in the years to come to make a contribution to Canada.
When we come to analyse the income of the average Canadian we realize that it is insufficient for him to give his children a decent standard of health and a decent standard of education. The Canadian federation of agriculture has stated that from 1930 to 1937, roughly eight years, the average net income per farm was $400.50 and the average income for industry was roughly $1,031. There is a great difference between the two incomes.
I think we must all realize that neither of these incomes is really sufficient to maintain the standard of health and education which is necessary for our people. Recently the dominion bureau of statistics made a study of the budgets of working-class families. This really was a striking exposure of the underprivileged position of most of our working families. They broke down the figures to show the amount spent by the average family upon food. A family with a yearly income of around $775 would spend roughly seventeen

War Appropriation Bill
cents per person a day upon food. A family earning $1,000 would spend roughly twenty-one cents; a family earning $1,200, twenty-three cents; a family earning $1,400, twenty-five cents; a family earning $1,600, twenty-seven cents, and a family earning $1,850, twenty-eight cents.
Early in 1940 the Canadian Medical Association, with the best dietetic advice it was possible to obtain, drew up a series of menus for families of different sizes. These menus listed only necessary food substances. For the average family of from four to five they placed the cost per person a day for food requirements at twenty-six cents. A family earning $775 per annum can spend only seventeen cents per person a day upon food, and we must get up into the income bracket of $1,400 before we find a family able to spend twenty-five cents per person a day for food. When we find that our farmers are earning roughly $400 per annum and our industrial workers $1,031, we begin to realize that no people earning these sums are able to provide the necessary food to give their families a decent standard of health.
We cannot get away from these facts and I do not think they can be disputed. If they can, I should be only too glad to know it. This investigation shows that one year ago about 85 per cent of our population were forced to live below the minimum standard of nutrition. I fear that now a far greater number of our people will have to live that way. If that is so, how can we expect the people of this nation to make the maximum effort which they would like to -make when they have not sufficient in their daily rations to provide the health and strength necessary for a maximum effort. These things simply cannot be done. When these huge appropriations are being made, I feel that the government should inaugurate a health programme in this country, and they should set aside an appropriation for education as aid to such provinces as are needing it. Certain things by way of legislation are needed to get the income of our people up to that level where health can be maintained1.
Before very long we may have an opportunity to discuss the need for legislation to provide a floor below which agricultural prices cannot drop, so that our agricultural population may be brought up to a proper standard. Then in the industrial world there are certain orders in council passed by this government which have limited and which will limit the right of our working people to work and to obtain a better wage which the increased earnings of industry warrants. This afternoon the Minister of Labour (Mr McLarty) said that 14873-1X5*
later on we would have an opportunity of discussing certain orders in council which have had the effect of restricting wages. There is no doubt that the matters which I have mentioned are part of our war effort. I feel that with this appropriation bill the government is being one-sided in its war effort. It has not given sufficient thought to nor has it brought forward sufficient legislation for these things which I have mentioned.
There is no doubt that to-day we as a nation need greater vision in looking toward the future. We cannot expect to have the benefits of democracy if we are not willing to put into the lives of our people those things which are so necessary to encourage democracy and to make it flourish and function. I feel that in the advisers of our government to-day there is too strong a representation of business and industry. In -the governmental committee assisting in the war effort where are the educationalists? Where are the members of the medical profession? Where are those people who have a broader and wider vision? This committee which is aiding the government in its war effort is made up almost exclusively of business interests. As long as that is so, the war effort of the government will continue to be directed more or less in that one direction and will not be directed into those various channels so necessary in a fight for democracy.
This makes it quite easy for those people interested in industry to talk loudly of their patriotism. But patriotism consists of more than mere words. To-day patriotism is like charity, it should begin at home, in and around the lives and homes of our own people. Those of us who are prepared to take this course have as great a claim to patriotism as any of those interested in the business side of the war effort, who are continually wanting to concentrate and focus the attention of the nation upon those matters, to the detriment of others.
Before a bill of this kind is passed, the ordinary people of this country should have a better knowledge of what is going to be the foreign policy of this government with regard to the future. There is no doubt whatever in the minds of most of us that we are in this war because Britain is in this war. We have not through the years had a very definite foreign policy, and a great many people these days are wondering greatly what will be our future foreign policy. Are we in our future foreign policy to be guided and directed by those same business interests which to-day are guiding and directing this war effort; if so, what will be their interest, and how will it guide the destiny of this nation?
War Appropriation Bill

Some hon. members may have read a book by John McCormac called "Canada-America's Problem", in which he says:
Canada's foreign policy has . . . consisted largely of a refusal to have any. This almost purely negative attitude has involved the surrender of any right to fashion in peace the imperial policies for which the dominion has to fight in war.
And again:
The poorest voter in London's east end has more control over Canada's foreign policy than a member of Canada's parliament.
We the common people, before we see the appropriation of such sums as this for war, want to know what is going to be the foreign policy of this government in the future. Are we to be committed to more wars because those who are standing behind the government's war effort to-day can see further profits in involvement in further wars? These are some of the things I feel we cannot pass over without more information.
There was a famous man of the United States who at one time was facing a crisis which was as great perhaps as that which faces us to-day. I am speaking of Abraham Lincoln, who said at the time of the civil war:
I have two great enemies, the southern army to the south of me and the financial institutions in the rear, and of the two the one in the rear is my greatest foe.
As one of the common people I would say this, and I think there are thousands who would say it with me, that if business and industry are to control entirely our war effort, and if they are to concentrate upon the business side of things for the profit which will be gained from it, rather than allocating some of this money to education and other services of which the people are in need; if this business concentration is to guide the destiny of Canada in the future as apparently it is guiding it to-day, then I think we can bring the words of Lincoln up to date by saying, "We have two great enemies, Hitler to the front of us and the financial institutions in the rear, and of the two the one in the rear is our greatest foe". That is, from the point of view of the common people, the financial institutions are at the present time our greatest foe.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) say on March 5:
One of the war aims of the allies is the defence and preservation of democracy. Of course, all forms of government are handicapped by imperfections inherent in their contingent and human nature. For that very reason should they not ever strive after justice, honesty, and sound and true freedom, which cannot possibly be derived from the favouritism and ambition of exploiters, who invariably subordinate the welfare of the people to their own interests?

I can certainly endorse those words. I feel that to-day we are fighting against Hitlerism and fighting also for the preservation and extension of democracy. I do not want this war effort to be a one-sided war effort. I want it to be an effort which will truly preserve democracy so that in the years to come we people will be able to say that here in Canada, "a loftier race than ere the world hath known shall rise with the flame of freedom in their soul and the light of knowledge in their eyes."
I feel that in the name of the people whom I represent I must oppose this appropriation bill because it neglects some of the fundamental things for which we as a nation believe we are fighting.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to
call attention to three or four matters on clause 2 of this bill, which is to appropriate $1,300,000,000 for the war. The larger the amount of the appropriation, the less likelihood there is of its being well spent. The main purposes of the bill are to provide for home and overseas defence and for the matters set out in paragraphs (b), (c) and (d). Three weeks ago I asked the government if they would take into consideration the works which Canada has established for the defence of this north American continent. We decided to spend a large amount on defence works on the Pacific coast long before the United States had any idea of passing the lease-lend bill. At that time, two years before the war, Canada was spending about twice as much on postage stamps as on defence by sea and air.
Under the lease-lend act of the United States, Canada ranks with Britain, and I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that with the passing of this appropriation bill we should revise our clause 2 herein and also our elaborate system of exchange and the work of the foreign exchange control board, and that an agreement should be made between Canada and the United Ctates for the parity or near parity of our dollar with the United States dollar, notwithstanding any law, statute, usage or custom to the contrary. As I said, Canada, by a ruling handed down by the attorney general of the United States, is to receive equality of treatment with the mother country under the lease-lend measure. I feel that the people of this country from coast to coast are willing to make any scarifices to win this war, and I believe they will support this appropriation if they believe the money is essential to the winning of the war.
I believe there has been too much talk altogether, judging by the statements I have heard from the government, about home

War Appropriation Bill
defence. Home defence is not as essential here as it is in Britain. Britain is only a few minutes by air from the continent of Europe and is within easy range of German air power, bombers and flame parachutes.
I believe that under this bill the Canadian government should take up with Washington the question of making an arrangement to recoup the people of Canada for the expenditures they have made on defences by land, sea and air. When all is said and done, what is the basis of Canada's foreign policy? As a matter of fact, we have never had any foreign policy at all. As to defence policy, the Minister of National Defence two or three years ago-we had only one Minister of National Defence then-laid down two cardinal principles of our defence. One was home defence, and the other was to protect our neutrality against any foreign power that might want to use our harbours and ports for non-neutral purposes to attack the United States. With very little change that is the policy of the government to-day. So I say that the government should take this matter up with Washington, and I believe they should pay part of this bill, because the purpose of most of this is to protect the neutrality of Canada in case the United States is attacked.
Another matter, Mr. Chairman, I referred to the other night. Mr. Wendell Wilkie got a glorious reception to-day in Toronto-the leading recruiting district of Canada; they came there from all over Canada to seek recruits for units spread all over Canada for Canada's forces. Mr. Willkie could tell this parliament and the people of Canada some things which his country has done for its soldiers that we have not done for ours. The first relates to national insurance for soldiers. This parliament has adopted a measure of insurance for those civilians who stay at home. Then why should not the soldiers who are going overseas to risk their lives for the people of Canada be insured also? The last time this resolution was being discussed I proposed to put on Hansard something which was not allowed to be inserted, though hon. members may notice that in the same day's issue three or four treatises of ministers were included. A bill for national insurance for soldiers which the president signed at Washington three weeks ago insures every soldier in the United States for a large sum of money. The policy contains a_ clause which protects his dependents and provides for contingencies-demobilization, unemployment, sickness after the war, and all that kind of thing. The United States had a form of insurance during the last war. It saved^ the taxpayers large sums of money in pensions and assisted the men when demobilization came. I believe we should
have a national form of insurance for our own soldiers. Toronto insured for one thousand dollars all its soldiers in the last war.
Another reason why I am suggesting it is this. I have here a form of insurance contract whioh every soldier has to sign who, when he goes to war, has an existing policy with any insurance company in Canada. I might say first, as hon. members may be aware, that it is impossible for a Canadian soldier, or for that matter a Canadian civilian travelling overseas, to remain insured under any policy purchased since September, 1939, if he leaves the confines of the Dominion of Canada and the continental United States of America, unless he is prepared to pay an exorbitant additional premium. If that extra premium is not paid, and death should occur, the insurance company are liable only for the return of the premiums plus three per cent. Further, if the soldier should die from any cause whatsoever within six months after his return to Canada, a death claim will not be paid.
I have here a copy of the uniform war clause contained in all Canadian war policies issued at the present time. The soldier's policy, unless he can pay the additional premium, is practically vitiated. I believe that the government would have been well-advised if, in place of some of the expenditures provided for under this bill, they had inserted in the estimates under a national insurance plan for soldiers, a small amount to protect the lives of the soldiers who are going overseas. My view is that there should be an immediate investigation by a committee into the matter. I wrote about it to the inspector of insurance, Mr. Finlayson, because I believe that in view of the small number of casualties which we have had in this war as compared with the last war, the premiums charged by Canadian companies are exorbitant and should be inquired into by this parliament, in the interests of the soldier, of this country, and of the future of insurance in Canada. The life insurance companies are not doing their duty.
Just one or two other matters. I may say that so far as the soldier is concerned, Mr. Willkie could tell the people of Canada' what his country is doing for its soldiers travelling on the railways. While recently on a train,
I noticed that troops coming from Petawawa are required to pay $1.25 to $1.50 for a meal, and similar rates apply to men travelling from one camp to another all over Canada. Under the United States government the railways have had to come to time on the rates for soldiers' meals. On the Union Pacific a day's meals can be had for ninety cents-twenty-five cents for breakfast, thirty cents for lunch, thirty-five cents for dinner, or three meals for
War Appropriation Bill

ninety cents, or for less than the price of one which on our railway systems, is being charged soldiers who receive $1.30 a day.
Another tiring that Mr. Willkie could have told us is what the United States is doing about soldiers' fares. How did it come about that Canada, where it is estimated 700,000 passes are issued annually by the railways, has not enough money, under clause 2 of this bill, to transport its soldiers? How did it come about that a country which is paying out $4,000,000 a day cannot spend the equivalent of one-half hour's expenditure to give its soldiers free transportation? Every day on the trains I see men, connected with almost every department of the public service, travelling on annual passes, many in contravention to the Railway Act. Why does the government not do as the United States and other countries have done-compel the railways to carry the soldiers free? In addition, in the United States they copied what was done in the last war by the city of Toronto, where soldiers travelled without charge on the street-cars: it is not done in this war, but some arrangement should be made by the government with the municipalities for free transportation of troops who live in the large cities and have to travel long distances from the suburbs to the place of recruitment or to a camp, and the federal power should pay for it.
I have here some tables of railway fares, and they are exorbitant. The rates paid by soldiers are, sometimes one-third more than those at which, from time to time, civilians can travel on special occasions from the maritimes, for instance, to central Canada. I called this to the attention of the railway commission and asked them to stop this discrimination of their own volition as the Railway Act empowers them to do, but nothing was done. They would not do anything. They seem to have also the parliamentarian's religion, the policy of following the line of the least resistance and doing nothing. Everybody in Ottawa seems to be afflicted with it and with this virus of inaction. I might mention that out of this vote of $1,300,000,000 large sums will be paid the railways for transporting troops vast distances across Canada to camps which never should have been erected; yet apparently we cannot afford any money for the particular purpose I have mentioned. Illegally, as I contend, an order was passed prohibiting hitch-hiking and making it a military offence, over parliament's head. I have here a letter from the Ontario minister of highways, Hon. T. B. Mc-Questen, in which he says that he had not seen the order to which I referred, but that (Mr. Church.]
neither his department nor the Ontario government had ever at any time objected to hitch-hiking by soldiers. Civilians are permitted to hitoh-hike, and why should soldiers be discriminated against by some officers who have federal cars at camps? The order is illegal, and I hope it will be at once withdrawn. The railways inspired such an order of prevention. Under this vote an adequate amount should be included to pay transportation for soldiers on leave. In spite of the hundreds of thousands of dollars provided under this vote for the transportation of troops, I venture to say that when the monthly bills come in, twice the amount of money will be due to the railways on this account as in the last war.
At Camp Borden on Saturday five or six young men were sent to gaol for fake railway tickets. It is a disgrace to the people of Canada that this should be so, when 700,000 passes are yearly issued on the railways and some military officers have passes, and in view of the huge sums which the railroads will be getting under this vote, increasing their receipts-according to a financial column in the morning paper the other day-from forty to forty-five per cent as a result of the war and the transportation which they are paid to give, to all these camps across Canada. Fancy taking Ontario's troops to Winnipeg and Petawawa! I see that there are some Toronto soldiers, the Toronto Scottish, at Three Rivers. Others have to go out to the coast and the maritimes. Why move them all over Canada and put money in the pockets of the railways, in defiance of economy, the nature of the military situation, training purposes, good business, and the interests of the soldier? These young men of whom I have spoken deserve a break, because they were first offenders of whom the commanding officer at Barrie at the trial spoke most highly, and said he would take these -men back. At the -trial it came out that this was the result of the two railways' influence in stopping hitch-hiking. I do not see any members of parliament hitch-hiking, or any members of the government, or any of the seven hundred thousand people in Canada or officers of camps, who have passes. The Duff report of 1931 sets out at page 154 reforms which should be made in transportation passes and suggests changes in the whole system, but nothing has been done.
This vote is too large; the railways are getting too much; those matters should be looked into; we should -have a rescinding of the illegal order to stop hitch-hiking, and camp officers should ignore it. Leave is refused if a soldier has not enough money for

War Appropriation Bill
fares. An inquiry should be held into the [DOT] whole matter by a committee of the house, and into all these matters.

speechtext:
I wish to ask the Minister
of National Defence whether instructions have been given to officers commanding army units and other army officers to observe by-laws passed by municipalities for the purpose of preventing fires, and to cooperate with the civil authorities in avoiding fire hazards on army premises.
There have been a considerable number of fires in premises occupied by the army in different parts of this country. There were fires in the exhibition building in Fredericton, which was destroyed; in the O'Regan building in Saint John, which was destroyed; in the exhibition building in Saint John, which was destroyed; in a building in Yarmouth and in other buildings not only in the maritimes but in other parts of Canada.
I am bringing the matter to the minister's attention because I recently saw a report, dated January lt>
last, made by Colonel E. J. Mooney, building inspector for the city of Saint John, to the common council of that city. In the course of that annual report he said:
Another local condition I would like called to the attention of the council is the way the defence department is doing work without taking out building permits, which means that I have no authority to inspect the work done.
I spoke to Major Blake, commanding officer of engineers at headquarters of military district No. 7, and he informed me that the engineers could design and build according to their own ideas and local civic authorities had no jurisdiction. As a result all kinds of infractions of the building and fire laws and common sense have been made and on several occasions due to lack of common knowledge such things as furnaces in our exhibition buildings were placed on thin concrete slabs on top of wood floors, stovepipes carried through wood partitions without proper insulation and as a result our fire department had to be called out to extinguish fires in these buildings.
About a month after that report was made, the exhibition buildings in Saint John were burned down. As far as those buildings are concerned, my information is that in the exhibition building proper there were five stoves, and the chimneys of those five stoves were all connected with a seven-inch jointed stove pipe that must have been about forty feet long running up through a fibre board false ceiling to the upper floor, and then to the roof. In the blind space between the ceiling and the floor above, there must have been a great accumulation of dust, and there is information that the dust fell down from the floor into this space when the upper floor was swept. There were a great many panes
of glass out in the front of the building-as a consequence, there were plenty of blobs of dust floating around, and the chimney, without any sort of insulation, must have been red hot at times, which would set fire to this dust.
The board of fire underwriters looked into the matter and made two reports. I am informed that the first report showed that there were great fire hazards and they were ordered corrected, and the report went on and said that they had been corrected. A second report, however, was subsequently made which said that not only were the former hazards replaced but they were greatly increased. Not only was the exhibition building destroyed and a number of other buildings adjoining it, but some valuable equipment was destroyed. One man lost his life, and if the fire had happened at night instead of in the middle of the day, in all probability a great many men would have lost their lives.
At the present time in the barracks square back of that building there are many temporary huts. My information is that they are constructed of light inflammable wood with pitch roof, false fibre board ceilings, and with jointed stove pipes running up through to the peak, wfith no insulation whatever; that some of these huts must accommodate a great many men, and that at any time there are likely to be further fires in these huts.
In addition, I should like to ask the minister whether these fires were investigated. If they were, who investigated them? After they were investigated, were reports made to the department, and can these reports be tabled? Further, was any action taken in consequence of these reports, and was any disciplinary action taken against any officer in consequence of these fires breaking out?
There is another matter to which I wish to refer. I do not wish to trouble the minister too much, but could he outline to us how promotions are made among officers in the army in Canada? There have been a great many promotions. This matter must be of considerable importance to the Minister of Finance. How' are these promotions made? Is it a matter of time; does a man have to serve a certain length of time in one rank before he is promoted to another? I may tell the minister that there is some dissatisfaction. among officers who volunteer and go overseas and do not get promotion, while those who stay home do, in many instances get promotion. Might not some way be evolved whereby promotions at home might be a little slower,, even though the officers have to take on some other duties?

Regarding the fires, I wish my hon. friend had drawn my attention to this matter so that I could have obtained a report from the quartermaster-general as to the matters of considerable detail1 with which he has dealt in connection with construction at Saint John. I cannot tell him at this moment whether or not actual orders go out requiring cooperation with the civic authorities. I do remember that in the case of one of the fires to which the hon. gentleman refers, high praise was given some of the military personnel who assisted in putting out the fire and in saving the equipment.
With regard to the matter of fires, I can only say to the hon. gentleman that I will make inquiries and give an answer either to him personally or to this committee. The practice is to hold courts of inquiry, and the findings of those courts are placed before the officers concerned, after which action is taken. I cannot give particulars at the moment; I remember the Yarmouth fire and the one at Saint John. Those are the two that have been brought particularly to my attention. I can assure the hon. gentleman, although I imagine I hardly need to do so because I believe he knows himself, that the district engineer officer at Saint John, Captain Blake, is an experienced officer who would not, I think, wilfully or carelessly put up buildings which did not conform to proper requirements with regard to fire hazards. However, I shall be glad to look into the matter and see if there has been any negligence or lack of care.
With regard to the matter of promotions, let me say to my hon. friend that promotions are made on the recommendation of the commanding officers concerned. These recommendations are passed upon by the district officer commanding, and then they come to national defence headquarters for approval.
With respect to staff appointments, as I think I have already told the committee, these appointments are made, after examination, by the selection board at national defence headquarters, based upon recommendations which are received from all over Canada as to officers in each district who are regarded as suitable for promotion or appointment to particular staff positions. These reports are gone over thoroughly, and the selection board itself makes the selection on the merits of the case. Although I should be disappointed to hear of it, at the same time I should welcome any instance my hon. friend can give me in which promotions have not been made on the basis of merit, whether in connection with the forces in Canada or for overseas service. If there is one thing I have tried to emphasize, and I think the officers

[DOT] at headquarters have tried to emphasize, it has been that particularly at a time like this, and, as far as that goes, at all times, promotions must be based on merit. I want to say to my hon. friend what I stated to the committee the other day, that I am a bit radical in respect of this matter of service and seniority. There are instances when it seems to me promotions ought to be made even over the heads of more senior officers, when the merit and the services of particular men may warrant that being done; and I wish to say to the hon. gentleman that I think this principle does govern the selections which are made at national defence headquarters. I had a talk on the same subject with the district officers commanding when they were here, and I would very much expect that this policy is being followed.
I say again that if my hon. friend has any instance in which he thinks an injustice has been done, I should be glad if he would bring it to my attention, although I want to tell him that I am taking the only ground that a minister can take if he is going to administer an armed force; that is, to see to it that there is no interference from national defence headquarters with the responsibilities of officers commanding in connection with making recommendations for promotions. We hold the officers commanding responsible for the administration of their units, and if we attempt to thrust upon these officers people whom we at headquarters may think desirable men, then the chain of responsibility is broken.

The report stated that during the past few months Halifax had been a cesspool of preventable disease; that there had been a large number of cases of diphtheria, influenza and meningitis. When I heard the hon. member for North Battleford say that Halifax

War Appropriation Bill

I think, on health services, I felt that someone ought to bring this matter to the attention of the ministers concerned, particularly because so many boys from all over Canada are at Halifax at the present time. What is being done by the Dominion of Canada to supplement the exceedingly inadequate health services in that city?
The story I read in yesterday's New York Times, dealing with the report made by this group who were sent to Halifax by the Rockefeller institute, made me feel not only alarmed but ashamed that such a condition could exist at this time in a Canadian city. You cannot easily give them immunity from some of these diseases, and I am asking the Minister of Pensions and National Health what he can tell us about the situation at Halifax, whether any steps have been taken to deal with the serious condition which has developed in that city during the past several months.

I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. During 1940 many of us did our

I should like the estimated cost in dollars and cents, say for the past year, (a) of free transportation and (b) for men taking such leave if they had been required to pay a one-way fare for the first three hundred miles, and then had been given free transportation for the balance of their trip. I do not think there is any other action which would do more toward bolstering the morale of these men or improving their attitude toward the government and toward those officials who are placed in control over them. I believe it would improve their opinion respecting the general attitude of the government toward those men who are willing to make the greatest sacrifice of all.
Any action the government might take would have a splendid effect upon the morale of parents, brothers and sisters at home who might see again their loved ones who may never come back. The men who are to do the fighting do not know what they are going into over there. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe there is some misapprehension in connection with this matter, and I am confirmed in that view by what the hon. member has said. There have been all sorts of suggestions with respect to free transportation. Generally, the suggestion has simmered down to free transportation on embarkation leave, as it is called.
I do not think hon. members have a clear understanding of the procedure in connection with embarkation leave. The idea apparently in the minds of hon. members is that men who are taken to a port should be allowed a few days' leave before sailing, so that they might go to their homes, and that on account of their being a great distance from their homes free transportation should be allowed. The committee will understand that it is impossible, from the point of view of our

War Appropriation Bill

conducting a war, for us to give even the slightest indication as to when- men are going to embark.
What we endeavour to do is this: When men are moved from their home stations, and when we have in mind that it is quite possible those men are being moved for the purpose either eventually or in a comparatively short time of going overseas, the custom is at such time to give what is called- embarkation leave. That embarkation leave is not a serious financial burden to a man. It would be serious if he were 'taken from the port of embarkation, or from a point near the point of embarkation, and sent back to his home. Generally speaking, however, embarkation leave is given some time before embarkation, and given when the men are at points comparatively close to their homes.
As I say, we endeavour to meet the convenience of the men, as far as possible. I did have one serious complaint from Calgary, where it was pointed out that men had not been given sufficient notice, with the result that they felt they could not take embarkation leave, and go home-to Edmonton, I believe-and get back in time. But that was a case which arose through misunderstanding, and I believe that had there been proper administration, those men would have got their leave. As I say, however, the rule is to give embarkation leave at a time when they are near their homes, and, if necessary, we see to it that an advance is made in their pay in order that they may have the benefit of that leave. But we do not give free transportation. The rules with regard to transportation state that the men travel on a one-way fare.
This question of transportation has been raised frequently, and I do not propose to make any extended statement with regard to it to-night. Let me say, however, that I have gone over the records for the last war, and I find no instance of free transportation having been granted, except in one special case in connection with harvest leave. I am speaking from memory, but I believe what I say is correct. Free transportation was never granted, as part of a soldier's privilege, for the purpose of visiting his home. It has been granted only in the event of some special mission, such as the one I indicated as harvest leave, when men were sent home, free of charge, because it was believed to be in the interests of the country so to do.
The granting of free transportation simply means the addition of that much to a soldier's pay; that is what it means. In this war we have increased the pay of the men, and we have provided for dependents' allowances as well. But that is nob all. In this war the
(Mr. Ralston.]
dollar buys considerably more than it did at the time of the last war. Therefore there has been a substantial increase both ways, both in the amount paid to the men and in the amount the dollar will buy.
I might as well say to my hon. friend that I see no likelihood of the government's reconsidering the decision it has made-and the matter of providing free transportation for men going on leave has been brought to our attention repeatedly. Rather we would endeavour to meet the convenience of the men, as far as possible, and see to it if we can, that leave is granted in such a way that it will entail comparatively small expense if a man wishes to visit his home.

The minister did not seem to be clear as to where the idea for free or assisted transportation came from. He stated it did not exist in the last war, but there were two reasons for that, and there may have been many others. The system of training in this war is different from that carried on in the last. We have specialized groups located in different areas for training. Generally speaking, a man who enters the army service corps will go to Petawawa, as would a man entering the artillery. This would be the situation no matter in what part of Canada he might enlist. If a man joins the tank corps, he goes to Camp Borden. If a man is in the infantry, the chances are that he will train fairly close to home, but that does not apply to the special units and most of the men are in these units. The result is that many men are long distances from home.
I had an example of this coming down on the train when I met a man who had joined the forestry corps in Nanaimo, British Columbia, and who had been sent to Valcartier. He said that was where they were training the forestry units. At the end of his period of training he was given leave and he found himself faced with an impossible situation. If it had not been for the assistance given by some of his wife's people, he would not have been able to go back to Nanaimo at the end of one year's service.

War Appropriation Bill
Second, there are large bodies of men being placed on garrison duty. We have the third and fourth divisions disposed of on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and a man may find himself posted on one coast, perhaps many miles from his home. At the end of a year these men are given a furlough, but it is no good to them unless they can raise the money to go back home.
There is a changed situation to-day, and that is why the demand has arisen.
What I said applies also to our sailors to some extent and to our airmen, but I mention sailors particularly because every time I happen to be travelling between here and home there are sailors on the train, either sailors going from Halifax to Calgary to their homes, or returning to Halifax from Calgary. The railway fare is, of course, veiy high. They get only one leave a year, and a good deal of the pay they have saved up is absorbed by the railway fares to take them home.
Those who are advocating government assistance in the matter of transportation have in mind, not free transportation, but assisted transportation. Certainly a man who is stationed 1,000 or 1,500 miles away from home should receive assistance in buying his transportation back home. I know the minister has quite a problem there and that it is not easy of solution, but perhaps a special rate could be worked out with the railways, or else when a man is granted his furlough, if his home was beyond a certain distance, let us say 500 miles, he might be given assistance to cover any distance beyond that.
Certainly the situation to-day is not a happy one for a man who finds himself 1,500 or
2,000	miles from home; it is a situation I knew quite a few men to be faced with before Christmas, and if the man has not the means, he cannot take advantage of his furlough to visit his loved ones back home. I hope the minister will give consideration either to working out an arrangement for giving assistance above a certain mileage, or to arranging with the railroads for a rate of one cent a mile to help these men when they go home on furlough.

The minister has stated that transportation was not given in the last war, but once the soldier got overseas, free transportation was given. Unquestionably the soldiers are being kept in Canada for a longer period in this war than in the last. I was overseas for four years
during the last war, and during that whole time I do not ever remember having to pay my transportation. I was in Canada for a period of five months only. To-day, however, there are many soldiers who have been in Canada for a year or more. There is also this question of the soldiers being moved from the west to the east, and when they are granted leave we know that it is impossible for ninety-nine out of a hundred of them to pay their fares back home if they live any distance away.
If we cannot get free transportation for the soldiers, some form of pool rate should be worked out so that soldiers who have been moved from one end of Canada to the other should not be penalized. In addition to a special rate, some form of pool rate should be worked out. It is not the soldier's fault that he is moved from Calgary to Petawawa. Contrast the soldier in that position with one whose unit is stationed just outside the city only a few miles from his home and who can get home for a few cents. It is a very unfair situation. If we cannot get free transportation, there should be a special rate, and on top of that a pool rate.
So far as embarkation leave is concerned, there should be free transportation on embarkation leave. Some soldiers have told me that it would not help very much because often they have only 'three hours' notice before they embark and leave is not granted, but in some instances it is granted, and in such instances free transportation should be provided.
The minister has stated that he is not sure where the demand comes from. The demand has been caused by public opinion. It is not coming from just any one section; public opinion throughout Canada is absolutely behind the demand for free transportation, and I think it is the least we can do for a man who has enlisted and is prepared to sacrifice his life for his country. He should at least be given an opportunity to go home and see his wife and family, but under present conditions that is not possible in many instances unless the soldier is prepared to commit a crime. If he has not the money to pay his fare home, he will take the train to some nearby point and then go on by freight, which is listed as a crime. In this way we are breeding crime within the army and causing discontent. So I hope that the government will seriously consider ways and means by which special rates can be given so that the soldier can travel at least as cheaply as the civilian. As it is now, we find that civilians get special fares -while the soldier has to pay a higher rate. That is absolutely unjust. Finally, I suggest that the government should give consideration to establishing a pool rate.

speechtext:
I have been awaiting an opportunity to ask the Minister of National Defence a question with regard to the equipment of units training in Canada. When the minister dealt with the formation of the armoured division he said he was not going to give information with regard to their equipment. That is a matter the minister must decide. If he sees fit not to give that information, we certainly will not press for it. I think, however, it would be a good thing if the minister could see fit to give us information with regard to the equipment of units training in Canada.
fMr. Ralston.]
The other day the minister gave the house some advice; he said that hon. members frequently were in a position to give information to the public and help the government along. With that I entirely agree, but hon. members must have that information in order to be able to impart it. I do not think there is any subject on which I am asked questions more often than on this very matter of equipment. The reason for that is, I think, that among one's constituents there are many who have sons, brothers or acquaintances training with units in different parts of Canada, and in their communications these men pass on to our constituents statements with regard to the equipment available.
There is no doubt that one reason for originally deciding on the thirty-day training was a shortage at the time of the necessary equipment. There is little doubt in my mind that to some extent the equipment situation has improved, but here we have infantry units and specialized units of many kinds. For instance, there are four or five motorcycle regiments training in Canada. I do not know whether they have the necessary motor cycles for their training, but certainly a technical unit of that description cannot get very far without motorcycles and the necessary facilities for keeping them in operation. In addition, there are signallers, anti-tank regiments, anti-aircraft companies and so on. These are all technical units, and without equipment they cannot get on with their training.
Would the minister see fit to give us some information in this regard? He will remember quite well that we of the opposition did not feel satisfied last year in respect of the amount of information forthcoming with regard to Bren guns. It did not seem to me then, and certainly it does not seem to me now, that it is reasonable to withhold information with regard to the output of Bren guns. Certainly infantry units cannot get on with this most necessary part of their training if they have not Bren guns in numbers greater than simply those necessary to look at, as unfortunately was the situation some time ago. We should like to be informed that it has improved. As yet the minister has not explained the reason for his extraordinary omission with regard to the entire change in the John Inglis contract when he spoke on November 15. He spoke two weeks after that change had taken place, and my recollection is that the space occupied in Hansard in referring to the Bren gun was only about three-quarters of an inch. He dismissed it very lightly. It was not until the news more or less accidentally tumbled out that the

public in Canada knew anything about the complete change in the John Inglis company contract.
The minister will no doubt explain to us why in that speech of November 15 when he, as Minister of National Defence was describing the progress his department was making in the war effort, he did not refer to that. If, however, the minister chooses to take the line that information with regard to this equipment in some detail would be of assistance to the enemy, again we must content ourselves, and remembering that the responsibility is on the government we must make what answer we may to the constituents who ask us for information.

speechtext: I should say the Minister of National Defence would describe to the house such change in the John Inglis company's contract that considerably increased any production which would be forthcoming from then on.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The increase in production was, as I understand it, very largely an increase in production on account of British orders.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Under the new regime,
the new contract, from what the Minister of Munitions and Supply tells us there is a possibility of turning out tens of thousands of guns.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Tens of thousands of guns in a long time. But I was dealing with the deliveries. I had given my hon. friend the number up to the end of September. This is what I say at page 149 of Hansard:
Regarding Bren guns, I have given my hon. friend the number up to the end of September. I am not giving the number delivered each week, but it is a figure which I must say is most satisfactory having regard to what was planned on when production started at the plant. These weekly deliveries are increasing steadily and by the end of the first year of production we expect to have three times as many guns delivered as were called for by the contract.
Is there anything in the world which calls upon me to tell the house that my colleague is negotiating a new contract with the John Inglis company in order to reduce the cost of them? The production which was being increased was with regard not only to the Bren gun, but to other items. The Browning machine gun was one which had not been previously manufactured there at all. I plead guilty to anything for which I am to blame, but I do not take the responsibility for this. I am sorry if my hon. friend feels I should.
With regard to the matter of equipment, I shall be pleased to have a statement prepared, if the matter may stand over.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not wish to detain the committee at all, but it does seem to me there was a lack of frankness on the part of the administration with respect to the new set-up of the John Inglis company.
War Appropriation Bill

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend had brought up the matter when my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply was here, because he made the statement about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I know he did. He told the house how it came out, first of all by an error on the part of his secretary, which I think was not quite cricket, and, second, through the inquisitiveness, if I may so describe it, of a newspaper. I do not think the country feels the government was quite candid with respect to this whole Bren gun situation. The new contract was made while the house was still in session, and we were not apprised of what was going on. I do not think that was candid. I am not, however, going to stir up that old sore now. It is not worth while.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I must take issue with my hon. friend about the matter of frankness.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I find the Minister of National Defence never admits anything, and the Minister of National Defence for Air is much more candid. He tells us his difficulties, and we forgive him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And he gets away with it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But at the same time, I do not propose to plead guilty to this.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: All right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With respect to the training of specialists and tradesmen in the vocational schools, what steps are taken? I understand the vocational school in Toronto is now being used by the army. I do not believe that was brought out in the minister's statement.
I believe that in the long run he would find it in the interests of economy to get the railways to cooperate in some way in connection with the matter of troops going on leave. A great many suggestions have been made, and it is my belief that over a period of years the government would find it an economy.
One further point. Fire underwriters have said that the fire protection at Camp Borden is a model for all other military camps in Canada. I suggest that hon. members having camps in their districts should see the methods by which the huts at Camp Borden are protected from fire. There is a stand pipe in each hut, and a permanent hose connection. The underwriters' association have reported favourably on that method of fire protection.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I understand my hon.
friend is referring to the trades school being set up in Hamilton.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And in Toronto.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We are providing for the training of about 2,000 men. There will be a normal three months' course, and for certain trades that course will be lengthened, depending upon the degree of specialization required.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: For the ordnance corps.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, for the ordnance corps particularly, and for the army service corps.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What are the methods of recruiting for that course?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We are not recruiting for the course. Men are enlisted, and are then sent for training.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They are selected.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We are not recruiting for the course. The men are recruiting into the army, and then taken there for training in their special trades.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Did the Minister of Labour obtain figures showing the number of men and women who have taken or are now taking industrial training, dividing the information into the four classes of priority? Perhaps the minister could also tell us what arrangements have been made for training men in shipbuilding. Then the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services might tell us whether the government has in contemplation the training of merchant seamen. The Minister of Munitions and Supply announced the other day that Canada was to build her own merchant ships. Many losses have been suffered by the British merchant marine, and it may be only a matter of time until merchant seamen may be required from Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We are doing some training of those who will be absorbed into the industry, but the industry itself is doing most of the necessary training and upgrading of its own employees. While we give basic training in the use of machines used in shipbuilding, the real training can be done only in the shipbuilding yards. I shall give the figures asked by my hon. friend as far as I have been able to obtain them, and there will be an opportunity later on to give them in a more complete form. The total number in the war emergency and youth training plans at the end of February was 11,423. Of that number, those in the industrial classes totalled 6,351.

War Appropriation Bill

speechtext: Is that the number in training or those who have been trained?
